mainTopic: Things said in any language: סוטה, וידוי מעשר and קריאת שמע, and quiet תפילה
overview: The amud opens with the last words of the long משנה listing things that may be said in any language. The גמרא learns from 'וְאָמַר הַכֹּהֵן' that פרשת סוטה may be said in any language. A ברייתא adds that the כהן tells the סוטה, in a language she understands, why she drinks, what she drinks from, and how she became impure, so that nobody will speak badly of the מים המרים. The גמרא then learns וידוי מעשר from סוטה through the shared plain word 'saying'. אביי defends this against רב זביד's comparison to the לויים. This leads to רבי שמעון בן יוחי's teaching that a person says his praise quietly and his pain loudly, so that others will pray for him. The גמרא then defends his teaching that תפילה is quiet to spare sinners shame, just as the חטאת and the עולה share one slaughtering place. Finally, רבי and the חכמים argue whether קריאת שמע may be said in any language, and each side explains the words 'שמע', 'והיו' and 'הדברים'. The amud ends as the גמרא begins to suggest what רבי holds. The suggestion is about language, and it continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The final words of the משנה
steps.stepSummary: The משנה ends by saying the people went back and slept in their own lodging place.
steps.simpleTranslation: And they slept in their place.
steps.whatsHappening: These are the last words of the long משנה. It finishes its story of the people, who went back and slept where they were staying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This line only closes the story the משנה was telling. Right after it the גמרא starts, and it goes back to the first item on the משנה's list, פרשת סוטה.

keyTerms.meaning: and they slept, stayed the night
in their place, where they were staying
the basic teaching that the גמרא explains

phrases.english: and they slept in their place.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the משנה that was started earlier on the daf.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The משנה's story ends with the people sleeping in their lodging place.

steps.title: How do we know the סוטה section may be said in any language?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens by asking for the source that פרשת סוטה may be said in any language.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: The section of סוטה, from where do we know it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins and asks for a source. The משנה said פרשת סוטה may be said in any language, and the גמרא wants to know how we know that.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'מנלן' asks for a source in the תורה. It does not doubt the rule. It wants the פסוק that the rule is built on. This sets up the answer in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: the discussion that explains the משנה
the section the כהן says to the סוטה (warning and oath)
from where do we know it?

steps.confusionAlert: The question does not ask whether סוטה is said in any language. That was already stated in the משנה. It only asks for the source.

phrases.english: GEMARA: The section of sotah — from where do we know it?
phrases.notes: The question is about the משנה's rule that this section may be said in any language.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the first item on the משנה's list and asks for its source.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The פסוק that shows פרשת סוטה may be said in any language.

steps.title: The source: 'And the כהן shall say to the woman'
steps.stepSummary: The word 'וְאָמַר' teaches that the כהן may speak in any language he speaks.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: 'And the כהן shall say to the woman.' This means in any language that he speaks.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a פסוק. The plain word 'and he shall say' teaches that the כהן may speak in any language.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק does not require any exact fixed words or a holy language. It just says 'say'. So the גמרא learns that any language is fine, as long as the כהן is truly speaking to her.
steps.whyThisMatters: 'Saying' to someone means speaking so they understand. This leads straight into the ברייתא, which says she must understand what she is told.

phrases.english: As it is written: "And the priest shall say to the woman"
phrases.notes: במדבר 5:21

phrases.english: in any language that he speaks.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 2.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The word 'וְאָמַר' in the פסוק teaches that the כהן may speak in any language.

steps.title: A ברייתא: four things the כהן tells her in a language she understands
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says the כהן tells the סוטה, in a language she understands, why she drinks, what she drinks from, why she is impure, and how she became impure.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: We tell her, in any language she understands, why she drinks, from what she drinks, for what she became impure, and in what way she became impure.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא with four things the כהן must tell her. It also stresses that it must be in a language she understands.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 3 spoke about the language the כהן speaks. This ברייתא adds the woman's side: she must understand it. It also lists what the conversation must include. The next lines explain the four items one at a time.

keyTerms.meaning: we make her hear, we tell her

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
We inform her
in any language that she understands,
for what reason she drinks,
and from what she drinks.
For what she became impure,
and in what way she became impure.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן מַשְׁמִיעִין אוֹתָהּ בְּכׇל לָשׁוֹן שֶׁהִיא שׁוֹמַעַת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the 'any language' rule and adds that she must understand it and what must be said.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The כהן tells the סוטה four things in a language she understands: why she drinks, from what, why she is impure, and how.

steps.title: Explaining why she drinks and what she drinks from
steps.stepSummary: She drinks because of קינוי and סתירה, and she drinks from a plain clay vessel.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why does she drink? Because of the warning and the being alone together. From what does she drink? From a clay bowl.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא starts explaining its list. It answers the first two items: the reason she drinks and the vessel she drinks from.
steps.deeperAnalysis: She drinks because of קינוי (her husband's warning) together with סתירה (being alone with that man). Without both, there is no drinking. She drinks from a מקידה של חרש, a simple clay vessel, not a fancy one.

keyTerms.meaning: the husband's warning not to be alone with a certain man
being alone with that man after the warning

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא teaches that the כהן explains the process to her in her own language. She drinks because of קינוי plus סתירה, from a plain clay vessel.
steps.confusionAlert: 'עַל מָה הִיא שׁוֹתָה' is not repeated by accident. The ברייתא repeats its own list item and now answers it.

phrases.english: For what reason does she drink?
on account of the matter of warning and seclusion,
and from what does she drink?
From a bowl of clay.

steps.triggerLanguage: עַל מָה הִיא שׁוֹתָה עַל עִסְקֵי קִינּוּי וּסְתִירָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the first two items in the ברייתא's list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: She drinks because of קינוי and סתירה, and from a clay vessel.

steps.title: What led to the sin, and whether it was willing
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues: the כהן tells the סוטה that levity and immaturity bring a person to sin. He also tells her it matters whether she sinned by accident or on purpose, by force or willingly.
steps.simpleTranslation: What made her impure? Things of light-headedness and childishness. And in what way did she become impure? By accident or on purpose, by force or willingly.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא from step 4 keeps going and answers its last two points: why she became impure, and how she became impure.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Why' is answered with the cause: frivolous, immature behavior leads to sin. 'How' is answered with a distinction the כהן must explain: an accidental or forced act is different from a willing one.

phrases.english: On account of what did she become impure?
On account of matters of levity and immaturity.
And in what way did she become impure?
Unwittingly or intentionally,
by force or willingly.
phrases.notes: The word 'or' in square brackets is part of the corrected wording.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list in the ברייתא after step 5 answered the first two points.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The כהן explains that levity leads to sin, and that an accidental or forced act is different from a willing one.

steps.title: Why the כהן explains all this
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא gives the reason for the explanation: so people will not speak badly of the bitter water.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why all of this? So that people will not give the bitter water a bad name.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא ends by explaining why the כהן must tell her all these details.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If she sinned by accident or by force, the water will not harm her. Without this explanation, people who saw a guilty woman unharmed might say the water does not work. The explanation protects the reputation of the מים המרים.

keyTerms.meaning: The bitter water the סוטה drinks

steps.whatToRemember: The כהן tells the סוטה, in a language she understands, why she drinks, what she drinks from, why she is impure, and how. This way nobody will doubt the bitter water.

phrases.english: And why all of this?
So as not to put out a bad name
phrases.notes: If she sinned by accident or by force, the water won't affect her, and people might wrongly decide the water doesn't work.

phrases.english: about the bitter water.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reason behind everything listed in steps 4 to 6.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Everything is explained so the bitter water will not get a bad name.

steps.title: Source for saying וידוי מעשר in any language
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא moves to the next item in the משנה and asks how we know that וידוי מעשר may be said in any language.
steps.simpleTranslation: The declaration of tithes: from where do we know it may be said in any language?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finished with סוטה. Now it asks for the source of the next item on the משנה's list.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה listed things that may be said in any language. The גמרא now looks for the source for וידוי מעשר, the declaration a person makes after giving all his tithes.

keyTerms.meaning: The declaration that one has given all his tithes

phrases.english: The declaration of tithes: from where do we know this?
phrases.notes: The משנה listed this together with פרשת סוטה as things that may be said in any language.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the same kind of question as step 2, now about the next item in the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source that וידוי מעשר may be said in any language.

steps.title: Learning 'saying' from סוטה
steps.stepSummary: The verse about וידוי מעשר says 'and you shall say.' We compare it to the 'saying' by סוטה, which may be in any language.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: 'Then you shall say before the Lord your God: I have removed the holy things from the house.' And we learn 'saying' from סוטה: in any language that he speaks.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a גזירה שוה: the same word 'saying' appears by וידוי מעשר and by סוטה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 3 showed that 'ואמר' by סוטה means in any language. Since the verse of וידוי מעשר also uses 'ואמרת,' the same rule carries over.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Saying,' the shared word in the comparison
Comparing two places in the תורה that use the same word

phrases.english: As it is written:
"Then you shall say before the Lord your God:
I have removed the holy things from the house,"
phrases.notes: דברים 26:13

phrases.english: And we learn 'saying' from סוטה,
phrases.notes: By סוטה the verse says 'ואמר הכהן,' which we saw in step 3.

phrases.english: that it is in any language that he speaks.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 8.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A גזירה שוה of 'אמירה' from סוטה teaches that וידוי מעשר may be said in any language.

steps.title: רב זביד: why not learn from the לויים?
steps.stepSummary: רב זביד asks אביי why we don't compare 'saying' to the לויים, who said the blessings and curses in לשון הקודש. Then וידוי מעשר would also have to be in לשון הקודש.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב זביד said to אביי: But let us learn 'saying' from the לויים! Just as there it was in the holy tongue, so too here it should be in the holy tongue!
steps.whatsHappening: רב זביד challenges the comparison. He points to a different verse with the word 'saying' that would give the opposite result.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'saying' also appears by the לויים at הר גריזים and הר עיבל, and they spoke in לשון הקודש. If the word alone decides, why compare to סוטה and not to the לויים?

keyTerms.meaning: The Levites, who announced the blessings and curses
Just as there, so too here

phrases.english: Rav Zevid said to Abaye:
But let us learn 'saying' from the Levites!
phrases.notes: דברים 27:14, 'וענו הלוים ואמרו.'

phrases.english: Just as there it was in the holy tongue,
so too here it should be in the holy tongue!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב זְבִיד לְאַבָּיֵי, וְלֵילַף אֲמִירָה מִלְּוִיִּם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the גזירה שוה used in step 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: The choice to compare וידוי מעשר to סוטה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Another verse with 'saying' (the לויים) requires לשון הקודש, so the comparison could point the other way.

steps.title: Plain 'saying' matches plain 'saying'
steps.stepSummary: אביי answers that plain 'saying' is compared to plain 'saying,' like סוטה. It is not compared to a verse that says 'answering and saying,' like the לויים.
steps.simpleTranslation: We compare a plain 'saying' to a plain 'saying,' and we do not compare a plain 'saying' to 'answering' and 'saying.'
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers רב זביד and defends the comparison to סוטה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By וידוי מעשר and by סוטה, the verse only says 'saying.' By the לויים it says 'answering and saying,' so that verse is less similar. We compare to the closest match, so the comparison to סוטה stands.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Answering,' the extra word in the verse of the לויים

steps.whatToRemember: וידוי מעשר may be said in any language. It is learned from סוטה because both verses use plain 'saying.' The לויים verse says 'answering and saying,' so it is not a matching comparison.

phrases.english: We derive a plain 'saying'
from a plain 'saying,'
and we do not derive a plain 'saying'
from 'answering' and 'saying.'
phrases.notes: The verse of the לויים has both words: 'וענו' (they answered) and 'ואמרו' (they said).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב זביד's challenge in step 10.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the wording of the verses
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any verse with the word 'saying' could be used, including the לויים.
steps.terutzMaskana: A plain 'saying' is compared only to another plain 'saying,' so וידוי מעשר follows סוטה and may be said in any language.

steps.title: Say your praise quietly and your disgrace loudly
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא of רבי שמעון בן יוחי teaches that a person says his praise quietly, learned from וידוי מעשר, and his disgrace loudly, learned from מקרא ביכורים.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is taught: רבי שמעון בן יוחי says: A person says his own praise in a low voice and his disgrace in a loud voice. Praise quietly: we learn this from וידוי מעשר. Disgrace loudly: we learn this from מקרא ביכורים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that fits אביי's point that plain 'saying' and 'answering and saying' are different. Plain saying is quiet, and answering and saying is loud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In וידוי מעשר a person says he did everything right. That is praise, and the פסוק only says 'and you shall say,' so it is said quietly. In מקרא ביכורים the פסוק says 'answer and say,' meaning out loud, and the text tells of the hard times of our ancestors. So it counts as 'disgrace' said loudly.

keyTerms.meaning: his disgrace, something embarrassing about him
the passage read when bringing first fruits

phrases.aramaic: תַּנְיָא, רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי אוֹמֵר:
phrases.english: It is taught: Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai says:
A person says his own praise in a low voice
and his disgrace in a loud voice.
His praise in a low voice:
we learn it from the declaration of tithes.
phrases.notes: There he says he did everything right, and the פסוק only says 'and you shall say,' plain saying.

phrases.english: His disgrace in a loud voice:
we learn it from the reading of the first fruits.
phrases.notes: The פסוק there says 'you shall answer and say' (דברים 26:5), meaning out loud, and it retells hard times from our past.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא, רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא that matches אביי's distinction between plain 'saying' and 'answering and saying.'
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Praise of oneself is said quietly, like וידוי מעשר; disgrace is said loudly, like מקרא ביכורים.

steps.title: But we pray quietly so sinners won't be embarrassed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how one could say his disgrace loudly, when רבי שמעון בן יוחי himself taught that תפילה is quiet to protect sinners from embarrassment.
steps.simpleTranslation: Should a person really say his disgrace loudly? But רבי יוחנן said in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחי: Why did the חכמים set up תפילה to be said in a whisper? So as not to embarrass people who sinned. For the Torah did not give a different place for a חטאת and an עולה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא. Saying your disgrace out loud seems to go against another teaching of the same רבי שמעון בן יוחי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: People confess their sins in their תפילה, so it is said quietly to spare them shame. The תורה does the same: a חטאת and an עולה are slaughtered in the same place, so nobody can tell who brought a sin-offering. This shows the תורה does not want a person's sins exposed, so how can disgrace be said loudly?

keyTerms.meaning: burnt-offering, brought even without a sin

phrases.english: And his disgrace in a loud voice?!

phrases.aramaic: וְהָאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי:
phrases.english: But didn't Rabbi Yochanan say in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai:
Why did they set up prayer to be said in a whisper?

phrases.aramaic: כְּדֵי שֶׁלֹּא לְבַיֵּישׁ אֶת עוֹבְרֵי עֲבֵירָה.
phrases.english: So as not to embarrass those who sinned.
phrases.notes: He means people who confess their sins while they daven.

phrases.english: For the verse did not give a separate place
for a sin-offering and a burnt-offering!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the second half of the ברייתא in step 12.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that a person says his disgrace loudly.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same תנא taught that sinners should not be embarrassed, which is why תפילה is quiet and a חטאת shares its place with an עולה. Announcing disgrace loudly contradicts that.

steps.title: Read it as 'his pain,' not 'his disgrace'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא changes the wording: a person announces his pain loudly, so the public will pray for him, as we learn from the מצורע who calls out 'impure, impure.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Don't say 'his disgrace'; say 'his pain.' As it is taught: 'And he shall call out: Impure, impure.' He must let the public know his pain, and the public will ask for mercy for him. And anyone who has something bad happen to him should let the public know, and the public will ask for mercy for him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by fixing one word in the ברייתא. What is said loudly is a person's pain, not his sins.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Sins should stay private, which is why תפילה is quiet. Pain is different: sharing it brings others to pray for you. A ברייתא learns this from the מצורע, who calls out that he is טמא, and widens it to anyone going through trouble.

keyTerms.meaning: don't say... rather say (a change of wording)
to make it known to the public

steps.whatToRemember: Keep your sins quiet, but share your pain. When the public knows, they can pray for you.
steps.confusionAlert: The answer does not say a person should announce his sins. It changes the ברייתא's word 'disgrace' to 'pain,' so the challenge about embarrassing sinners no longer applies.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for the practice of letting others know when someone is sick or suffering, so the community can daven for him.

phrases.english: Do not say 'his disgrace,'
rather say 'his pain.'
As it is taught: 'And he shall call out: Impure, impure':
phrases.notes: ויקרא 13:45, said about a מצורע.

phrases.english: he must make his pain known to the public,
and the public will ask for mercy for him.
And anyone to whom something bad happens
should make it known to the public,
and the public will ask for mercy for him.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא תֵּימָא גְּנוּתוֹ, אֶלָּא אֵימָא צַעֲרוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 13 by changing the wording of the ברייתא in step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Change of wording (לא תימא... אלא אימא)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to say a person announces his disgrace, including his sins, loudly.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא means his pain. Pain is shared loudly so others pray, while sins stay private.

steps.title: Quiet prayer protects sinners, like the shared place of חטאת and עולה
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן quotes רבי שמעון בן יוחי: תפילה is quiet so sinners are not embarrassed, just as the Torah gave the חטאת and the עולה the same place.
steps.simpleTranslation: Back to the statement itself: רבי יוחנן said in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחי: Why did they make prayer quiet? So that sinners will not be embarrassed. The תורה itself did not give a separate place to the חטאת and the עולה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the statement it quoted in step 13 so it can look at it on its own. רבי שמעון בן יוחי gives the reason for quiet תפילה and brings a source for it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person might confess his sins in his תפילה. If people prayed out loud, others would hear the confession. The תורה shows the same concern: a חטאת is brought for a sin and an עולה usually is not, but both are slaughtered in the same place, so a watcher cannot tell which one is being brought.

keyTerms.meaning: 'The thing itself.' The גמרא is returning to a statement it quoted earlier so it can discuss it directly.
A sin-offering, brought to atone for a sin
A burnt-offering, often brought as a gift, so it does not show that the owner sinned

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for why the עמידה is said quietly. It also shows a broader value of the תורה: avoid embarrassing a person who has sinned.

phrases.english: Back to the statement itself:
phrases.notes: This is the statement that was quoted in step 13. Now the גמרא looks at it on its own.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yoḥanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai:
Why did they institute prayer in a whisper?
So as not to embarrass those who sin.
For the verse did not make a separate place
phrases.notes: ויקרא 6:18

phrases.english: between a sin-offering and a burnt-offering.

steps.triggerLanguage: גּוּפָא, אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the statement about quiet תפילה that was only quoted in step 13, and now discusses it directly.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: תפילה is said quietly so sinners are not embarrassed. The תורה shows the same concern by giving the חטאת and the עולה one slaughtering place.

steps.title: The blood of the two offerings goes in different places
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: the blood of a חטאת goes on the top of the מזבח and the blood of an עולה goes on the bottom, so there is a visible difference.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is there really no difference? The blood is different: the blood of a חטאת goes up high, and the blood of an עולה goes down low!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the claim that nothing separates the חטאת from the עולה. The blood of each one is placed in a different spot on the מזבח.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי שמעון בן יוחי's proof depends on the two offerings looking the same. If their blood is placed in different spots, people could still tell them apart, and the sinner would be embarrassed anyway.

keyTerms.meaning: Above, on the upper half of the מזבח / below, on the lower half

phrases.english: And is there really no difference?
But there is the blood:
the blood of a sin-offering goes above,
and the blood of a burnt-offering goes below!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the proof in step 15.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the Torah made no distinction between the חטאת and the עולה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The blood is placed in different spots, so the two offerings are visibly different, and the sinner could still be recognized.

steps.title: Only the כהן knows where the blood goes
steps.stepSummary: The difference in the blood is seen only by the כהן, so the public does not find out.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, it is only the כהן who knows.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the blood difference does not embarrass anyone, because only the כהן doing the service knows which kind of offering it is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The concern is about the public seeing who sinned. The slaughtering place is where everyone can see. The blood work is done by the כהן at the מזבח, so the difference stays with him and is not public.

keyTerms.meaning: It is only the כהן who knows

phrases.english: There, it is the priest who knows.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 16.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits who notices the difference: it is not public.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Different blood placement would show everyone that this is a חטאת.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only the כהן sees the blood difference, so the owner is not publicly embarrassed.

steps.title: A חטאת is female and an עולה is male
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges again: a חטאת is a female animal and an עולה is male, which anyone can see.
steps.simpleTranslation: But there is a difference: a חטאת is female and an עולה is male!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second, more visible difference. Anyone looking at the animal could see whether it is female (חטאת) or male (עולה).
steps.deeperAnalysis: This difference is not hidden with the כהן. It is in the animal itself, which the public can see. So the earlier answer about the כהן does not work here.

phrases.english: But there is a difference:
a sin-offering is female, a burnt-offering is male!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After step 17 answers the blood question, this brings a new difference that the public can see.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that onlookers cannot tell a חטאת from an עולה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Whether the animal is male or female can be seen by anyone, so the sinner could still be recognized.

steps.title: The tail covers it
steps.stepSummary: The female animal's private area is covered by its tail, so whether it is male or female is not plainly seen.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, it is covered by the tail.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that you cannot easily see whether the animal is female, because the sheep's tail covers that area.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A sheep has a large, fat tail that hangs down. Because it covers the area that would show the animal's gender, bystanders cannot easily tell the חטאת apart from the עולה.

keyTerms.meaning: The fat tail of a sheep

phrases.english: There, it is covered by the tail.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 18.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows the difference is not actually visible.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Anyone could see that the animal is female.
steps.terutzMaskana: The tail hides the animal's gender, so the public cannot tell.

steps.title: A female goat has no covering tail
steps.stepSummary: The tail answer works for a female lamb, but a female goat has no long tail, so its gender can be seen.
steps.simpleTranslation: That works for a female lamb. But a female goat, what can you say?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the tail answer. A goat does not have a big tail, so a goat brought as a חטאת would clearly look female.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A חטאת can be either a female lamb or a female goat. The tail answer only covers the lamb. For the goat, the difference is still visible, so the sinner seems to be exposed.

keyTerms.meaning: 'That is fine': this answer works for one case, but not for another
What is there to say? What answer works here?

phrases.english: That works for a female lamb,
but for a female goat, what can be said?

steps.triggerLanguage: תִּינַח כִּבְשָׂה, שְׂעִירָה מַאי אִיכָּא לְמֵימַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 19 by showing a case where it does not work.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the tail hides the animal's gender
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A goat has no large tail, so a goat חטאת would visibly be female and could expose the sinner.

steps.title: Someone who brings a goat has embarrassed himself
steps.stepSummary: Whoever brings a goat instead of a lamb chose to be exposed, so the Torah does not need to protect him.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, he is the one embarrassing himself. He should have brought a female lamb, and instead he is bringing a female goat.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the last challenge. A person who brings a goat had the choice to bring a lamb and stay hidden, so any embarrassment is his own doing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תורה gave the sinner a way to stay hidden: bring a lamb, whose tail covers it. If he chooses a goat anyway, he gave up that protection himself. So the proof of רבי שמעון בן יוחי stands: the תורה set things up to protect the sinner.
steps.whatToRemember: תפילה is said quietly so sinners are not embarrassed. The תורה shows the same care by giving the חטאת and the עולה one slaughtering place. The blood is handled only by the כהן, a lamb's tail hides that it is female, and someone who chooses a goat has exposed himself.

phrases.english: There, he is the one who embarrasses himself,
for he should have brought a female lamb
and instead he brings a female goat.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 20 and closes the defense of step 15.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Places the responsibility on the person who chose to be exposed.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The goat case shows that the תורה did not fully protect the sinner.
steps.terutzMaskana: The תורה gave a way to stay hidden (a lamb). Someone who brings a goat chose to give that up, so the proof still stands.

steps.title: The idol-worship sin-offering must be a female goat
steps.stepSummary: The חטאת for עבודה זרה must be a שעירה, so the earlier answer about choosing a goat does not work there.
steps.simpleTranslation: A sin-offering for idol worship can only be a female goat. What can be said about that case?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the last answer. For the sin of עבודה זרה, the person has no choice: he must bring a female goat, and anyone can see it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 21 the גמרא said that a person who brings a goat chose to be exposed. That answer depends on the person having a choice. Here the תורה requires a שעירה, so the person did not choose to be exposed, and he is shamed anyway.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not enough / it will not do

phrases.english: A sin-offering for idol worship,
for which nothing will do except a female goat,
what is there to say?

steps.triggerLanguage: חַטָּאת דַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה דְּלָא סַגִּי דְּלָאו שְׂעִירָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer of Step 21 by finding a case where there is no choice.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer in Step 21 that the goat-bringer chose to be exposed.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: For עבודה זרה the תורה requires a שעירה, so the sinner is exposed without choosing it.

steps.title: Let him be embarrassed, so he gets atonement
steps.stepSummary: For עבודה זרה, the embarrassment is welcome, because it helps bring his atonement.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, let him go and be embarrassed, so that he will be forgiven.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that for the sin of עבודה זרה, the תורה does not try to hide the sinner. His shame is part of how he is forgiven.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule of hiding sinners is meant to spare them shame. For a sin as severe as עבודה זרה, the shame is not something to avoid. It is useful, because it helps his כפרה.
steps.whatToRemember: The תורה hid the חטאת by slaughtering it where the עולה is slaughtered, to spare sinners shame. For עבודה זרה, the shame itself helps bring atonement.

phrases.english: There, let him go and be embarrassed,
so that he will be atoned for.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 22 and closes the discussion.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Accepts the facts but says the concern does not apply in this case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought the תורה always protects a sinner from public shame.
steps.terutzMaskana: For עבודה זרה, the shame is wanted because it helps bring כפרה.

steps.title: Where do we learn that קריאת שמע may be said in any language?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the משנה's list and asks for the source that קריאת שמע may be said in any language.
steps.simpleTranslation: From where do we learn this about קריאת שמע?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the list of things that may be said in any language. It asks for the source for קריאת שמע, and the answer comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה listed קריאת שמע among the things that may be said in any language. The גמרא wants a פסוק that teaches this.

phrases.english: Shema, from where do we know?
phrases.notes: He means: how do we know that שמע may be said in any language, as the משנה says?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the חטאת discussion and returns to the משנה's list of things said in any language.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The פסוק that permits saying קריאת שמע in any language.

steps.title: "שמע ישראל" means any language you understand
steps.stepSummary: The word "שמע" (hear) teaches that קריאת שמע may be said in any language the person understands.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it says, "Hear, O Israel": in any language that you hear.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the source. Since the פסוק says "hear," any language you can hear and understand is acceptable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: "שמע" here is read as "understand." The main thing is that the person understands what he is saying, so any language he knows works.

phrases.english: As it is written: "Hear, O Israel",
phrases.notes: דברים 6:4

phrases.english: in any language that you hear.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 24.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: "שמע" means understand, so קריאת שמע may be said in any language you understand.

steps.title: רבי and חכמים disagree about the language of קריאת שמע
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא: רבי says קריאת שמע must be said as written, and חכמים say in any language.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: קריאת שמע must be said as it is written, says רבי. The חכמים say it may be said in any language.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא showing that the rule in the משנה is not agreed upon by everyone. רבי holds you must say קריאת שמע in its original wording and language.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה follows חכמים, who allow any language. רבי disagrees and requires the original text, in לשון הקודש. This sets up the next question about רבי's reason.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is written (in its original language)

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
Shema must be recited as it is written; these are the words of Rabbi.
And the Sages say: in any language.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows that the view in Step 25 is the view of חכמים, and that רבי disagrees.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי: קריאת שמע must be said in its original language. חכמים: in any language.

steps.title: What is רבי's reason?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רבי requires קריאת שמע in its original language.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason of רבי?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for רבי's source. This is a setup line, and the answer comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since "שמע" seems to allow any language, the גמרא wants to know what פסוק רבי relies on to require the original text.

phrases.english: What is the reason of Rabbi?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of רבי's view in Step 26.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The פסוק behind רבי's view that קריאת שמע must be said as written.

steps.title: "והיו" means the words stay as they are
steps.stepSummary: רבי learns from "והיו" that the words of שמע must stay as they are, in their original language.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says "and they shall be": as they are, so shall they be.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives רבי's source. The word "והיו" teaches that the words must remain exactly as they are, without translation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי reads "והיו" as "they shall remain in their original state." Changing the language would change the words, so translation is not allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: In their original state, as they are

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think רבי argues with the word "שמע." He simply uses a different word, "והיו," as his source.

phrases.english: The verse says: "And they shall be",
phrases.notes: דברים 6:6

phrases.english: as they are, so shall they be.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 27.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: "והיו" teaches that the words must remain in their original form, so they must be said in לשון הקודש.

steps.title: What is the source for the רבנן?
steps.stepSummary: After explaining רבי's source, the גמרא asks for the source of the רבנן, who allow any language.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the רבנן? (What is their source?)
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now turns to the other side of the argument and asks why the רבנן allow קריאת שמע in any language. This is a short setup question for the next step's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 28 gave רבי's reason ("והיו"). To be fair to both sides, the גמרא now wants the פסוק that supports the רבנן.

keyTerms.meaning: The Sages, the majority opinion (here called חכמים in the ברייתא)

phrases.english: And the Rabbis?
phrases.notes: This is short for: what is the source for the רבנן, who allow any language?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from רבי's source to the רבנן's source.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The scriptural source for the רבנן's view that קריאת שמע may be said in any language.

steps.title: The רבנן learn from the word "שמע"
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן learn from "שמע" (hear) that קריאת שמע may be said in any language you understand.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says "שמע": in any language that you hear (understand).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the רבנן learn their view from the word "שמע". "Hear" means "understand", so any language you understand is fine.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same teaching as step 25. Now it is placed clearly as the רבנן's side of the argument with רבי. So each side has its own word: רבי has "והיו", and the רבנן have "שמע".

phrases.english: The verse says "Hear",
phrases.notes: דברים 6:4

phrases.english: in any language that you hear.
phrases.notes: "Hear" here means a language you can understand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 29.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The רבנן learn from "שמע" that any language you understand is allowed.

steps.title: What do the רבנן do with "והיו"?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the רבנן: "והיו" is written in the פסוק, so how do they explain it?
steps.simpleTranslation: But for the רבנן too, isn't "והיו" written?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the רבנן. The word "והיו" is in the תורה for everyone, so what do the רבנן learn from it, if not רבי's rule?
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי used "והיו" to teach that שמע must stay in its original language. The רבנן must explain this word somehow. Otherwise it looks like the פסוק supports רבי against them.

keyTerms.meaning: But it is written! (introduces a challenge from a פסוק)

phrases.english: And the Rabbis too,
isn't it written "And they shall be"!
phrases.notes: דברים 6:6. This is the word רבי used back in step 28.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the רבנן using רבי's source.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view of the רבנן that any language is allowed.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: "והיו" exists in the Torah, and רבי reads it as requiring the original language. The רבנן must explain what the word teaches.

steps.title: The רבנן use "והיו" to teach the correct order
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן learn from "והיו" that you may not say שמע out of order.
steps.simpleTranslation: That word teaches that one may not read it out of order.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers for the רבנן. They use "והיו" for a different rule: שמע must be said in the order it is written, not backwards.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sides agree that "והיו" means "the words must stay as they are". The question is what part stays. רבי says the language must stay. The רבנן say only the order must stay.

keyTerms.meaning: That (word or פסוק) is needed for something else

phrases.english: That one is
phrases.notes: He means: that word "והיו" is used to teach this.

phrases.english: that one should not read it out of order.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 31.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redirecting the פסוק to a different teaching
steps.terutzHavaAmina: "והיו" would require the original language, which goes against the רבנן.
steps.terutzMaskana: For the רבנן, "והיו" only requires saying שמע in the correct order.

steps.title: Where does רבי learn the rule about order?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks where רבי learns that שמע may not be said out of order, since he used "והיו" for language.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי: where does he learn that one may not read it out of order?
steps.whatsHappening: Now the גמרא turns to רבי. He used "והיו" for the language rule, so where does he get the rule that שמע must be said in order?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא assumes everyone agrees that saying שמע out of order is not allowed. Since רבי used "והיו" for something else, he needs a different source for this rule.

keyTerms.meaning: From where does he learn it?

phrases.english: And Rabbi,
that one should not read it out of order, from where does he know it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Now that the רבנן have a source for the rule about order, the גמרא asks for רבי's source.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: רבי's source for not saying שמע out of order.

steps.title: רבי learns order from "הדברים"
steps.stepSummary: רבי learns the rule about order from the extra ה in "הדברים" ("the words" rather than just "words"). The רבנן do not learn anything from that ה.
steps.simpleTranslation: He learns it from "words" versus "the words". And the רבנן do not learn anything from "words" versus "the words".
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רבי learns from the extra letter ה in "הדברים". "The words" means these exact words in their exact order. The רבנן do not learn anything from that extra ה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק could have said "דברים" (words), but it says "הדברים" (the words). רבי reads that extra ה as a teaching about order. The רבנן do not treat the ה as a teaching, so they need "והיו" for the order rule.

keyTerms.meaning: It does not mean anything to them; they do not learn from it

steps.confusionAlert: Both sides agree you may not say שמע out of order. They only argue about which word in the פסוק teaches that rule.

phrases.english: He derives it
phrases.notes: He means רבי.

phrases.english: from "words" versus "the words."
phrases.notes: דברים 6:6. The extra ה ("the") points to these exact words, in this exact order.

phrases.english: And the Rabbis, "words" versus "the words"
does not mean anything to them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 33 and explains why the רבנן cannot use this source.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי learns the rule about order from the extra ה in "הדברים". The רבנן do not learn from that ה.

steps.title: What does רבי do with "שמע"?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי: "שמע" is written, and the רבנן learned "any language" from it.
steps.simpleTranslation: But for רבי too, isn't "שמע" written?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now challenges רבי the same way. The word "שמע" is in the תורה, so what does רבי learn from it?
steps.deeperAnalysis: This mirrors step 31. Each side must explain the other side's word. Here רבי must explain "שמע", which the רבנן used to allow any language.

keyTerms.meaning: But it is written! (a shorter form of הָא כְּתִיב)

phrases.english: And Rabbi too,
isn't it written "Hear"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Mirrors the challenge of step 31, now aimed at רבי.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי's view that שמע must be said in its original language.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: "שמע" is written, and it seems to allow any language you understand. רבי must explain what the word teaches.

steps.title: רבי uses "שמע" to teach that you must hear yourself
steps.stepSummary: רבי uses "שמע" to teach that you must say שמע loud enough for your own ears to hear it.
steps.simpleTranslation: He needs that word to teach: let your ears hear what comes out of your mouth.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers for רבי. He reads "שמע" literally, as "hear": you must say קריאת שמע out loud so that you hear your own words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The רבנן read "שמע" as "understand". רבי reads it as real hearing with the ears, which is a rule about how loud to speak. So for רבי, the word teaches nothing about language.

phrases.english: He needs that one for:
to make your ears hear
what you bring out of your mouth.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 35.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redirecting the פסוק to a different teaching
steps.terutzHavaAmina: "שמע" would allow any language, which goes against רבי.
steps.terutzMaskana: For רבי, "שמע" teaches that you must hear your own words.

steps.title: The רבנן hold that saying it without hearing still counts
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן do not need "שמע" for the hearing rule, because they hold that if you said שמע without hearing yourself, you still fulfilled the מצוה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the רבנן hold like the one who says: one who reads שמע and did not make his ears hear it has fulfilled the מצוה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the רבנן do not learn the hearing rule from "שמע". They follow the opinion that hearing yourself is not required to fulfill the מצוה, so the word is free to teach "any language".
steps.deeperAnalysis: This closes the circle. Each word now has a clear job on each side. רבי: "והיו" teaches language, "הדברים" teaches order, and "שמע" teaches hearing yourself. The רבנן: "שמע" teaches any language, "והיו" teaches order, and hearing yourself is not required to fulfill the מצוה.

keyTerms.meaning: They hold like the one who says

steps.whatToRemember: The argument about language comes down to how each side reads three words. רבי reads "והיו" as language, "הדברים" as order, and "שמע" as hearing yourself. The רבנן read "שמע" as any language you understand and "והיו" as order, and they hold that not hearing yourself still counts.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that one מצוה rule (the language of שמע) is tied to other rules, about order and about saying it out loud. Each side has to explain every word in the פסוק.

phrases.english: And the Rabbis hold like the one who says:
One who reads Shema
and did not make his ear hear has fulfilled his obligation.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why the רבנן do not share רבי's reading from step 36.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Pointing to a different halachic position that frees the word for another teaching
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The רבנן would also need "שמע" for the rule that you must hear yourself, so they could not use it for language.
steps.terutzMaskana: The רבנן hold that not hearing yourself still counts, so "שמע" is free to teach any language.

steps.title: The גמרא begins to suggest what רבי holds
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens with "Shall we say that רבי holds..." and sets up a proposed reading of רבי's position.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say that רבי holds...
steps.whatsHappening: This line sets up the next move. The גמרא is starting to suggest a conclusion about רבי's opinion, and the actual suggestion comes right after these words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי needed the word "והיו" to require that שמע be said in its original language. Now the גמרא begins to propose what this shows about רבי's general view of language. The full suggestion continues on the next amud. The word לֵימָא signals a suggestion that the גמרא will then examine.

keyTerms.meaning: Shall we say? It opens a suggested conclusion that the גמרא will then check.
He holds. It introduces someone's legal opinion.

steps.confusionAlert: לֵימָא is not a final ruling. It is only a proposal, and often the גמרא ends up pushing it away.

phrases.english: Shall we say
that Rabbi holds
phrases.notes: This is רבי יהודה הנשיא, the same רבי from the last few steps.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on רבי's reading of "והיו" (step 28), which requires the original language, and begins to infer what רבי holds more broadly about language.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The גמרא is starting to ask what exactly רבי's position is, based on how he reads "שמע". The full content of the suggestion continues past these words.
